# Writing and Debugging Functions {#sec-functions}



A teammate asks for the 30-day event rate at each of the five
HF-HOME sites, one number per site, for a Monday-morning slide. You
write a short function that filters to a site and summarizes the
outcome, loop it over a vector of site names copied from last
week's report, and build the slide from whatever comes back. The
slide shows 1 number where there should be
5: two sites print nothing, one prints the wrong
one twice, and nothing in the console says an error occurred,
because nothing errored. The bug is not in the data; HF-HOME's
canonical site labels are exactly `"Site A"` through `"Site E"`.
The bug is in four characters of casing and whitespace copied from
a source that writes them differently, inside a function that
returns nothing at all when a site matches zero rows, and inside a
loop that quietly discards whatever that function returns. Finding
it does not require rereading the function more carefully; it
requires tools built for exactly this, and this chapter is about
using them before the slide ships, not after someone asks why
Site D has no number.

::: {.bookepigraph}
```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```
*Debugging is twice as hard as writing the code in the first
place. Therefore, if you write the code as cleverly as possible,
you are, by definition, not smart enough to debug it.*

[Brian W. Kernighan and Rob Pike]{.smallcaps}, *The Practice of
Programming* (1999)
```{=latex}
\end{flushright}
```
:::




::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Where this chapter sits: functions are written while wrangling and analyzing, and debugging them is the skill that makes both stages trustworthy rather than merely fast.](14b-functions_files/figure-pdf/fig-functions-pipeline-1.pdf){#fig-functions-pipeline fig-align='center' fig-alt='Diagram of the analysis pipeline: six stages in order (Plan, Acquire, Wrangle, Analyze, Report, Share) above two bands that run under every stage (Version control and Environment). Highlighted for this chapter: Wrangle and Analyze.' width=100%}

::: {.callout-note title='In this chapter'}
**Reading time.** About 45 minutes.

**You'll need.** @sec-wrangling for the `dplyr` verbs this chapter
reuses, @sec-types for the messy site labels in the running
example, and @sec-testing-unit for the `tinytest` assertions the
last section connects to. The code uses:

```r
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(rlang)
```

and calls `tinytest` with its namespace. All three packages are
installed in this book's environment.

**You'll be able to.**

- Write a function with named arguments, defaults, and `...`, and
  say what it returns without writing `return()`.
- Explain what a closure captures and predict what happens when the
  data a closure captured changes after the closure was created.
- Choose between `purrr::map()` and a base `for` loop or `sapply()`
  for a given iteration, and say what each one does with an error
  or a missing result.
- Use `traceback()`, `browser()`, and `debugonce()` to find the
  line in your own function that produced a wrong answer, and know
  when `options(error = recover)` is the better tool.
- Raise an error with `rlang::abort()` that carries a class and a
  data payload, and read what `rlang::last_trace()` adds over
  `traceback()`.
- Test a function in isolation from the pipeline that calls it.

## Why write a function at all {#sec-functions-why}

The case for a function in a general-purpose program is reuse: a
function called from ten places saves nine copies of the logic. A
one-off data analysis calls almost nothing from ten places, so
that argument understates the case and, read uncharitably, seems
not to apply at all. The sharper argument is not about reuse; it is
about correction and verification. A computation written out
five times, once per site, is five places a bug can hide and five
places you must remember to fix it when the computation changes. A
computation written once as a function, called five times, is one
place to fix a bug and one place to write a test. The acronym for
this is DRY (don't repeat yourself), and the reason it survives as
advice is not elegance; it is that the alternative multiplies the
cost of being wrong by however many times you copied the code
before you noticed.

`site_event_rate()` below computes the 30-day event rate for one
HF-HOME site, joining the randomization table to the outcomes
table once outside the function and filtering inside it:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(dplyr)

hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")
read_hf <- function(file) {
  readr::read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, file),
                  col_types = readr::cols(patient_id = "c",
                                          .default = "?"))
}
hf_rand <- read_hf("randomization.csv")
hf_outcomes <- read_hf("outcomes.csv")
hf_events <- inner_join(hf_rand, hf_outcomes, by = "patient_id")

site_event_rate <- function(data, site_name) {
  site_data <- filter(data, site == site_name)
  if (nrow(site_data) > 0) {
    summarize(site_data, n = n(),
              event_rate = mean(event_30d, na.rm = TRUE))
  }
}

site_event_rate(hf_events, "Site A")
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       n event_rate
#>   <int>      <dbl>
#> 1   700      0.206
```
:::


Later in this chapter the function above turns out to have a bug.
That is deliberate: the point of writing it as a function is not
that this version is correct, but that when it is found to be
wrong, the fix is one edit in one place, and the five call sites
that use it are automatically fixed along with it. Five copies of
the `filter()`-then-`summarize()` logic, one per site, would need
five edits, made correctly, in the same afternoon, with no
mechanical way to confirm that all five were actually changed.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague argues that a function is not worth
writing for code that will run exactly once, on one dataset, and
never again. Under what condition are they right, and how often
does that condition actually hold for an analysis script?

**Answer.** They are right only if the code genuinely runs once,
with no bug ever found in it and no reviewer ever asking for a
variant. For most analyses that condition does not hold: an
exclusion is revised, a reviewer asks for a sensitivity analysis
on a second subgroup, or a bug is found after the fact and must be
fixed everywhere the faulty logic was pasted. 'Runs once' describes
how the script is invoked, not how many times its logic turns out
to matter; the same observation motivates testing an analysis
(@sec-testing-why).
:::

### Exercises

1. Below is the same site-level computation written three times,
   once per site, with a copy-paste error in the third copy (it
   filters on `event_30d == 1` instead of computing a rate). Rewrite
   it as one function called three times, and explain why the
   function form makes the error impossible to introduce silently
   in only one call.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
a <- filter(hf_events, site == "Site A")
a <- summarize(a, n = n(), event_rate = mean(event_30d, na.rm = TRUE))
b <- filter(hf_events, site == "Site B")
b <- summarize(b, n = n(), event_rate = mean(event_30d, na.rm = TRUE))
e <- filter(hf_events, site == "Site E")
e <- summarize(e, n = sum(event_30d == 1, na.rm = TRUE))
```
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
site_rate <- function(data, site_name) {
  site_data <- filter(data, site == site_name)
  summarize(site_data, n = n(),
            event_rate = mean(event_30d, na.rm = TRUE))
}
site_rate(hf_events, "Site A")
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       n event_rate
#>   <int>      <dbl>
#> 1   700      0.206
site_rate(hf_events, "Site B")
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       n event_rate
#>   <int>      <dbl>
#> 1   571      0.246
site_rate(hf_events, "Site E")
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       n event_rate
#>   <int>      <dbl>
#> 1   290      0.213
```
:::


The error in the pasted version (counting events rather than a
rate) is possible only because the third copy has its own,
independently editable body. Once there is one function, every
call shares the same body, so a mistake made while editing it would
show up at every call site, not silently at one of three.
:::

## Anatomy of an R function {#sec-functions-anatomy}

A function definition has four parts: a name to call it by,
arguments it accepts, a body that computes something from them, and
a value it returns. `site_event_rate` has two arguments, `data`
and `site_name`, neither with a default, so both must be supplied
at every call. Adding a default makes an argument optional:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
site_event_rate <- function(data = hf_events, site_name) {
  site_data <- filter(data, site == site_name)
  if (nrow(site_data) > 0) {
    summarize(site_data, n = n(),
              event_rate = mean(event_30d, na.rm = TRUE))
  }
}
site_event_rate(site_name = "Site B")
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       n event_rate
#>   <int>      <dbl>
#> 1   571      0.246
```
:::


A default is evaluated lazily: R does not compute `hf_events` when
the function is defined, only when the function is called and
`data` is needed and no value was supplied for it. This matters
when a default refers to another argument, as `...` (dots) does in
the next example. `...` collects any number of additional,
unnamed-in-the-signature arguments and forwards them, which is how
a wrapper function can pass extra options through to the function
it calls without naming every one of them in its own signature:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
summarize_outcome <- function(data, ...) {
  summarize(data, event_rate = mean(event_30d, ...))
}
summarize_outcome(hf_events, na.rm = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 1
#>   event_rate
#>        <dbl>
#> 1      0.224
```
:::


`na.rm = TRUE` is not an argument `summarize_outcome()` names; it
passes through `...` to `mean()` unchanged. The convenience has a
cost: a misspelled argument, `na.rn = TRUE`, is silently absorbed by
`...` and forwarded to `mean()`, which also does not recognize it
and silently ignores it, rather than erroring at the call where the
typo actually is. Prefer naming an argument explicitly over
catching it in `...` whenever the function has a small, known set
of options to expose.

**Implicit return.** R returns the value of the last expression
evaluated in the function body; `return()` is needed only to exit
early, before the last line, typically from inside a condition.
`site_event_rate()` above never calls `return()`; its value is
whatever its final `if` evaluates to, which is why the branch with
no `else` is dangerous: when the condition is false, the `if`
itself evaluates to `NULL`, and that `NULL` is what the function
returns, with nothing marking it as a special case.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
is.null(site_event_rate(hf_events, "nonexistent site"))
#> [1] TRUE
```
:::


A function that reaches the end of its body with nothing left to
evaluate also returns `NULL`, invisibly; this is almost never the
intended value and is one of the two or three most common sources
of a `NULL` that propagates quietly into something downstream
(the other common source is exactly what happened above, a
conditional with no `else`).

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**An `if` with no `else` is a `return(NULL)` with no evidence that
you meant to write one.** Writing the `else` branch explicitly,
even if only to raise an error or return `NA`, turns a silent
default into a choice you can see later, in the function and in a
diff.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** `f <- function(x, verbose = FALSE) { if (verbose) print(x); x + 1 }`
is called as `f(5)`. What does it print, and what does it return?

**Answer.** It prints nothing, because `verbose` defaults to
`FALSE` and the `print(x)` branch is skipped. It returns `6`: the
function's value is the value of its last expression, `x + 1`,
regardless of what the `if` above it did or did not print. The
`if (verbose) print(x)` line is evaluated for its side effect
(printing) and its value, here invisibly `NULL` when `verbose` is
`FALSE`, is discarded because it is not the last expression in the
body.
:::

### Exercises

2. Write `event_rate_or()`, which takes `data`, `site_name`, and a
   third argument `default` with no default value of its own set
   in the signature, and returns `event_rate_or()`'s usual
   computation when the site has rows, or `default` when it does
   not. Call it once supplying `default = NA_real_` and once with no
   third argument at all, and explain the second call's error in
   terms of lazy evaluation.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
event_rate_or <- function(data, site_name, default) {
  site_data <- filter(data, site == site_name)
  if (nrow(site_data) == 0) return(default)
  mean(site_data$event_30d, na.rm = TRUE)
}
event_rate_or(hf_events, "nonexistent site", default = NA_real_)
#> [1] NA
event_rate_or(hf_events, "nonexistent site")
#> Error in `event_rate_or()`:
#> ! argument "default" is missing, with no default
```
:::


`default` has no default value, so it is a promise with nothing to
evaluate. The promise is never forced on the first call, because
`site_name` matches and `return(default)` is never reached. On the
second call the site is missing, `return(default)` is reached, R
tries to evaluate the promise for `default`, and finds no value
and no expression to compute it from, raising 'argument "default"
is missing, with no default'. Lazy evaluation means an unsupplied
argument with no default is not an error until the moment it is
actually needed.
:::

## Scoping and closures {#sec-functions-scoping}

R looks up a name a function uses, but does not define as an
argument or a local variable, in the environment where the function
was *created*, not the environment where it is *called*. This is
lexical scoping, and the environment a function remembers at
creation, together with the function itself, is a **closure**. The
distinction matters the moment a function returns another
function, which is exactly how a *function factory* works:
`make_rate_fn()` below takes a data frame and returns a function
that computes a site's event rate against that specific data frame,
without `data` appearing in the returned function's own argument
list:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
make_rate_fn <- function(data) {
  function(site_name) {
    site_data <- filter(data, site == site_name)
    mean(site_data$event_30d, na.rm = TRUE)
  }
}

rate_all_arms <- make_rate_fn(hf_events)
hf_events_uc <- filter(hf_events, arm == "Usual care")
rate_usual_care <- make_rate_fn(hf_events_uc)

c(all_arms = rate_all_arms("Site A"),
  usual_care_only = rate_usual_care("Site A"))
#>        all_arms usual_care_only 
#>        0.206422        0.218845
```
:::


Each call to `make_rate_fn()` creates a fresh execution environment
holding its own `data`, and the function it returns carries that
environment with it wherever it is called from next, which is why
`rate_all_arms()` and `rate_usual_care()` disagree about Site A
without either one taking a `data` argument that could be
confused with the other's. The binding is also frozen at the
moment `make_rate_fn()` evaluated its argument, not tied to
whatever the name `hf_events` happens to point to later:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
hf_events <- filter(hf_events, FALSE)   # pretend it got emptied
rate_all_arms("Site A")                 # unaffected
#> [1] 0.206422
```
:::


`rate_all_arms()` still reports the original rate, because
reassigning `hf_events` in the global environment changes what that
*name* points to, not the value already captured inside
`rate_all_arms()`'s own enclosing environment. This is reassuring
when you want it (a report built from functions created earlier in
a session is not retroactively altered by a later, unrelated
reassignment) and disorienting when you do not expect it (a
function you believe uses 'the current cleaned data' may in fact be
using a snapshot from whenever it was created, and `source()`-ing
the cleaning step again does not update it). The practical
consequence [@wickham2019advr, ch. 7] is to treat a closure's
captured data as a value fixed at creation, and to rebuild the
closure, not merely rerun the script around it, whenever the data
it closed over changes.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** `counter <- local({ n <- 0; function() { n <<- n + 1; n } })`
creates a function with no arguments. Calling `counter()` three
times in a row returns `1`, `2`, `3`. Where does the state `n` live
between calls, given that `counter()` has no arguments and no
global variable named `n` is visible at the top level?

**Answer.** `n` lives in `counter`'s enclosing environment, created
once by `local()` and captured when the function was defined. `<<-`
(superassignment) modifies `n` in that enclosing environment rather
than creating a local copy inside the call, so each call sees and
updates the same `n` the previous call left behind. `ls(environment(counter))`
shows `n` living there, invisible from the top level precisely
because `local()` discarded every other name created alongside it.
:::

### Exercises

3. Write `make_threshold_flagger(cutoff)`, returning a function
   that takes a numeric vector and returns `TRUE`/`FALSE` for values
   above `cutoff`. Create `flag_high_bnp <- make_threshold_flagger(1000)`
   and `flag_very_high_bnp <- make_threshold_flagger(5000)`, and
   show that changing `cutoff` in your own session afterward does
   not change either function's behavior.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
make_threshold_flagger <- function(cutoff) {
  function(x) x > cutoff
}
flag_high_bnp <- make_threshold_flagger(1000)
flag_very_high_bnp <- make_threshold_flagger(5000)
bnp <- c(200, 1200, 6000)

cutoff <- 0   # a later, unrelated reassignment of the same name
rbind(high = flag_high_bnp(bnp), very_high = flag_very_high_bnp(bnp))
#>            [,1]  [,2] [,3]
#> high      FALSE  TRUE TRUE
#> very_high FALSE FALSE TRUE
```
:::


Each call to `make_threshold_flagger()` created its own execution
environment with its own binding for `cutoff`, captured by the
function it returned. The later line `cutoff <- 0` creates or
changes a binding in the *global* environment, which neither
returned function looks up, because each one looks up `cutoff` in
the environment where it was defined, not in the caller's
environment.
:::

## Iteration: map over for {#sec-functions-iteration}

The opening story's bug is visible once the loop that computes it
is written two ways. The first version loops over site labels taken
from last week's report, which (as @sec-types established) mixes
the canonical `"Site A"` with casing and whitespace variants of
the other four, and assigns each result into a list with `[[<-`:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
site_labels <- c("Site A", "site b", "SITE C", " Site D", "Site E ")

for_result <- list()
for (i in seq_along(site_labels)) {
  for_result[[i]] <- site_event_rate(hf_events, site_labels[i])
}
length(for_result)
#> [1] 0
for_result
#> list()
```
:::


Four of the five labels do not exactly match a value in `hf_rand$site`,
so `site_event_rate()` returns `NULL` for each. Assigning `NULL` to
an element of a list with `result[[i]] <- NULL` does not store a
`NULL`; it *deletes that element*, shifting every later index down.
The loop above runs five times and the list it builds has length
1, with no error and no warning, because every
step of it, individually, is legal R. `purrr::map()` behaves
differently on the same inputs:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(purrr)

map_result <- map(site_labels, site_event_rate, data = hf_events)
names(map_result) <- site_labels
map_result
#> $`Site A`
#> NULL
#> 
#> $`site b`
#> NULL
#> 
#> $`SITE C`
#> NULL
#> 
#> $` Site D`
#> NULL
#> 
#> $`Site E `
#> NULL
```
:::


`map()` always returns a list the same length as its input, one
element per call, and a `NULL` result is stored as a `NULL`
*element*, visible at its own position with the label that produced
it still attached. The length-5 list with four visible `NULL`s is
not a nicer-looking version of the same information; it is the only
one of the two that shows you there is a problem, and where. `sapply()`
sits between the two, and its behavior depends on what it is given
back: when the results are not all the same type and length, as
here, `simplify = TRUE` fails silently and `sapply()` quietly
returns a list, exactly like `map()`; when the results would
simplify, `sapply()` returns a vector or matrix instead of a list,
and the type of what you get back changes depending on data you
have not seen yet. `map()` never does this: its return type is
part of its contract, not a function of the input.

@tbl-functions-iteration-compare summarizes the three.

| | `for` (`result[[i]] <- f(x[i])`) | `sapply()` | `purrr::map()` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Length of result | Can shrink if `f()` returns `NULL` | Can shrink the same way inside its own loop | Always equals `length(x)` |
| Return type | Whatever you built | Vector, matrix, or list, decided after the fact | Always a list |
| On an error | Stops the whole loop immediately | Stops the whole call immediately | Stops, unless wrapped (below) |

: Three ways to iterate a function over a vector, and what each
guarantees about what comes back. {#tbl-functions-iteration-compare}

A second, distinct hazard appears once the function can actually
raise an error rather than quietly returning `NULL`. The stricter
version below refuses an unmatched site instead of returning
nothing:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
site_event_rate_strict <- function(data, site_name) {
  site_data <- filter(data, site == site_name)
  if (nrow(site_data) == 0) {
    stop("no rows found for site '", site_name, "'")
  }
  summarize(site_data, n = n(),
            event_rate = mean(event_30d, na.rm = TRUE))
}
```
:::


A `for` loop over the same five labels stops entirely at the first
failure, having processed only the sites before it:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
for_strict <- list()
for (i in seq_along(site_labels)) {
  for_strict[[i]] <- site_event_rate_strict(hf_events, site_labels[i])
}
#> Error in `site_event_rate_strict()`:
#> ! no rows found for site 'Site A'
```
:::


`purrr::possibly()` wraps a function so that an error is caught and
replaced with a stand-in value, letting the iteration continue
through every element:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
safe_rate <- possibly(site_event_rate_strict, otherwise = NA)
safe_result <- map(site_labels, safe_rate, data = hf_events)
names(safe_result) <- site_labels
safe_result
#> $`Site A`
#> [1] NA
#> 
#> $`site b`
#> [1] NA
#> 
#> $`SITE C`
#> [1] NA
#> 
#> $` Site D`
#> [1] NA
#> 
#> $`Site E `
#> [1] NA
```
:::


`purrr::safely()` is the same idea with nothing discarded: instead
of a stand-in value, it returns, per element, a list with `result`
and `error`, so that a later step can see exactly which calls
failed and why, rather than only that they did. Reach for `possibly()`
when a stand-in value is an acceptable answer (a missing site
becomes `NA`, dropped from a later `mean()`); reach for `safely()`
when you need to inspect or report the failures themselves, for
example to tell a teammate which sites to investigate before
rerunning anything.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Confirm that `possibly()`'s catch is per-element, not all-or-nothing,
by counting how many of the five calls actually failed versus
succeeded:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
outcomes <- map_lgl(safe_result, ~ !identical(.x, NA))
c(succeeded = sum(outcomes), failed = sum(!outcomes))
#> succeeded    failed 
#>         0         5
```
:::


One call (the exact match, `"Site A"`) succeeds and four fail,
matching the four casing and whitespace mismatches in
`site_labels`; a `for` loop over the strict function would have
told you only that *something*, at or before the second element,
failed.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Why does the `for`-loop version earlier in this
section end up with a list of length 1 rather than, say, length 4
with the `NULL`s simply missing from wherever they would have gone?

**Answer.** `result[[i]] <- NULL` does not skip an assignment; it
removes element `i` if one exists, and inserts nothing if it does
not, so the list never grows past the last *successful* assignment
and nothing after it ever gets written. Here only the first of five
iterations (`"Site A"`) succeeds, so the list has exactly one
element (the second iteration deletes the nonexistent second
element, a no-op, and so do the third through fifth), and its
length tells you nothing about which four sites were skipped,
unlike `map()`'s length-5 list with the failures visible by
position.
:::

### Exercises

4. Rewrite the `for`-loop version from earlier in this section so
   that it has the same length guarantee as `map()`: preallocate the
   result list and assign by name rather than by
   `[[<-`-ing a possibly-`NULL` value into a growing list.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
for_fixed <- vector("list", length(site_labels))
names(for_fixed) <- site_labels
for (i in seq_along(site_labels)) {
  for_fixed[site_labels[i]] <- list(site_event_rate(hf_events, site_labels[i]))
}
length(for_fixed)
#> [1] 5
for_fixed
#> $`Site A`
#> NULL
#> 
#> $`site b`
#> NULL
#> 
#> $`SITE C`
#> NULL
#> 
#> $` Site D`
#> NULL
#> 
#> $`Site E `
#> NULL
```
:::


`vector("list", n)` preallocates a length-`n` list of `NULL`s, and
`for_fixed[site_labels[i]] <- list(...)` uses single-bracket
assignment with a one-element list on the right, which replaces an
element in place rather than deleting it. The length is now
guaranteed by the preallocation, independent of what any call
returns. The fix does not make the underlying bug (the mismatched
labels) go away; it only stops a second bug (the shrinking list)
from hiding the first one.
:::

5. Using `map_dbl()` instead of `map()`, compute the event rate
   (not a summary data frame) for every HF-HOME site using the
   correct, canonical labels, and explain why `map_dbl()` is a
   better choice than `map()` here if you intend to pass the result
   straight into `ggplot2`.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
canonical_sites <- sort(unique(hf_rand$site))
rates <- map_dbl(canonical_sites, function(s) {
  mean(filter(hf_events, site == s)$event_30d, na.rm = TRUE)
})
names(rates) <- canonical_sites
rates
#> Site A Site B Site C Site D Site E 
#>    NaN    NaN    NaN    NaN    NaN
```
:::


`map_dbl()` requires every call to return a length-one numeric
value and fails loudly at the first call that does not, rather than
returning a list that a plotting function would have to be
coerced out of first. For a result bound for a numeric column,
that extra constraint turns a type mismatch into an error at the
point it happens, rather than a confusing message three steps
later inside `ggplot2`.
:::

## Debugging your own code {#sec-functions-debugging}

The tools in this section assume an interactive R session; a book
rendered in one batch process cannot pause for you, so each tool is
shown as a console transcript rather than an executed chunk, except
where the condition can be reproduced and captured without a pause.
Read the transcripts as what you would see typing the same lines at
your own prompt, immediately after the error they follow.

**`traceback()`: after the fact.** When an uncaught error stops a
top-level command, R keeps the sequence of calls that led to it
until the next command runs. `traceback()` prints that sequence,
most recent call first, which tells you exactly which function in
the chain actually called `stop()` and which functions merely
called *it*:

```r
> site_event_rate_strict(hf_events, "site b")
Error in site_event_rate_strict(hf_events, "site b") :
  no rows found for site 'site b'
> traceback()
1: site_event_rate_strict(hf_events, "site b")
```

For a one-level call like this one, `traceback()` adds little; its
value grows with the depth of the call stack. Reusing the
wrapper from @sec-functions-iteration, where `possibly()` wraps
`site_event_rate_strict()` and `map()` calls the wrapper, a failure
three frames down produces:

```r
> map(site_labels, site_event_rate_strict, data = hf_events)
Error in site_event_rate_strict(data = hf_events, dots[[1L]][[2L]]) :
  no rows found for site 'site b'
> traceback()
4: site_event_rate_strict(data = hf_events, dots[[1L]][[2L]])
3: .f(.x[[i]], ...)
2: map(site_labels, site_event_rate_strict, data = hf_events)
1: (function() map(site_labels, site_event_rate_strict, data = hf_events))()
```

Frame 4, the one at the top, is where the error was actually
raised; everything below it is who called whom to get there. Read a
`traceback()` from the top down and stop at the first frame that is
your own code and not a library internal, because that is almost
always the frame whose assumption was violated.

**`browser()`: a breakpoint you write into the body.** Inserting
`browser()` as a line inside a function pauses execution there, the
next time the function runs, and drops you into an interactive
prompt with that call's local variables in scope:

```r
site_event_rate <- function(data, site_name) {
  site_data <- filter(data, site == site_name)
  browser()
  if (nrow(site_data) > 0) {
    summarize(site_data, n = n(), event_rate = mean(event_30d, na.rm = TRUE))
  }
}
site_event_rate(hf_events, "site b")
Called from: site_event_rate(hf_events, "site b")
Browse[1]> nrow(site_data)
[1] 0
Browse[1]> site_name
[1] "site b"
Browse[1]> unique(data$site)
[1] "Site A" "Site B" "Site C" "Site D" "Site E"
Browse[1]> c
```

The `Browse[1]>` prompt accepts ordinary R code evaluated in the
function's own execution environment, plus a few one-letter
commands: `n` steps to the next line, `c` continues to completion
(or the next `browser()`), and `Q` aborts back to the top level.
`nrow(site_data)` being `0` while `unique(data$site)` plainly does
not contain `"site b"` is the bug, seen directly rather than
inferred from a stack trace. Remove the `browser()` line once you
are done; it is easy to leave one in a committed file by accident,
and a reviewer who hits it has no idea why their session froze.

**`debugonce()`: the same pause, with nothing left behind.**
`debugonce(f)` sets a breakpoint at the start of `f()` for exactly
its *next* call, then removes itself, so you never edit the
function's source to insert or delete a `browser()` line:

```r
> debugonce(site_event_rate)
> site_event_rate(hf_events, "site b")
debugging in: site_event_rate(hf_events, "site b")
Browse[2]> n
Browse[2]> n
Browse[2]> nrow(site_data)
[1] 0
```

Each `n` steps one line further into the function body, stopping
before it executes, which is the natural tool when you want to
watch a function's state evolve statement by statement rather than
jump straight to one line. `debug(f)` is the same idea without the
'once': it stays armed until you call `undebug(f)`, useful while you
are actively iterating on a function but easy to forget and leave
armed afterward.

**`options(error = recover)`: a menu instead of a single pause.**
Set globally, it intercepts *every* uncaught error in the session
and offers a menu of frames to enter, rather than requiring you to
have predicted which function would fail and instrumented it in
advance:

```r
> options(error = recover)
> map(site_labels, site_event_rate_strict, data = hf_events)
Error in site_event_rate_strict(data = hf_events, dots[[1L]][[2L]]) :
  no rows found for site 'site b'

Enter a frame number, or 0 to exit

1: map(site_labels, site_event_rate_strict, data = hf_events)
2: .f(.x[[i]], ...)
3: site_event_rate_strict(data = hf_events, dots[[1L]][[2L]])

Selection: 3
Called from: eval(expr, p)
Browse[1]> site_name
[1] "site b"
```

It is the right tool when you do not yet know which function is at
fault, which is most real debugging; `browser()` and `debugonce()`
are the right tools once you already suspect one. Reset it with
`options(error = NULL)` when you are done, or it stays armed for
the rest of the session and surprises the next person who sees your
`.Rprofile`.

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
An agent can narrow where to look before you open the debugger
yourself.

> **Context.** `site_event_rate()`, defined in this session, returns
> a data frame for a site that matches rows and `NULL` otherwise.
> Called in a loop over `c("Site A", "site b", "SITE C", " Site D", "Site E ")`
> against `hf_events`, it should produce five rows, one per site.
>
> **Constraints.** Do not modify `site_event_rate()`. Investigate
> only by running read-only R code (inspecting values, not editing
> files) in this session.
>
> **Criteria.** For each of the five labels, report whether
> `filter(hf_events, site == label)` returns zero rows or more than
> zero, and if zero, show the exact character-by-character
> difference between that label and the value in
> `unique(hf_events$site)` it was meant to match.

*Failure mode.* An agent asked to 'fix the bug' instead might edit
`filter()` to match case-insensitively and call it done, which
repairs this one symptom while leaving the underlying problem, that
two different tables disagree on how to write a site name, both
undiagnosed and undocumented. *Check.* Confirm the agent's report
names all four mismatches (casing on two, leading or trailing
whitespace on two) rather than stopping at the first one, and that
it changed no file; the fix belongs in a decision about which table
is the source of truth for site labels, not in a case-insensitive
patch.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You set `options(error = recover)`, trigger an error,
and the menu lists five frames. Which one should you enter first?

**Answer.** Usually the deepest frame that is still your own code,
not a library internal. The error is raised at the bottom of the
list (the most recently called function), but the state most useful
to inspect is often one or two frames up, at the point your code
called into a library function with an argument that was already
wrong. Entering the exact frame that called `stop()` tells you what
failed; entering the frame above it often tells you why.
:::

### Exercises

6. Using `browser()`, find why `clean_sbp()` below returns `-99` for
   one value instead of `NA`. (Hint: the condition compares a
   trimmed string against an untrimmed one.)


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
clean_sbp <- function(x) {
  trimmed <- trimws(x)
  x[trimmed == "-99 "] <- NA
  as.numeric(x)
}
clean_sbp(c("120", "-99 ", "-99"))
```
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
Inserting `browser()` after the `trimmed <- trimws(x)` line and
inspecting `trimmed` shows it is `c("120", "-99", "-99")`: trimming
removed the trailing space, so `trimmed == "-99 "` (with a trailing
space in the pattern) matches neither element. The fix compares like
with like:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
clean_sbp <- function(x) {
  trimmed <- trimws(x)
  trimmed[trimmed == "-99"] <- NA
  as.numeric(trimmed)
}
clean_sbp(c("120", "-99 ", "-99"))
#> [1] 120  NA  NA
```
:::


The original bug produced `-99` silently surviving as a numeric
value indistinguishable from a real low blood pressure, exactly the
quiet, plausible-looking failure Habit 8 warns about.
:::

## Clear errors and warnings {#sec-functions-errors}

`base::stop()` raises a condition of class `"simpleError"` carrying
only a character message. `rlang::abort()` raises the same kind of
condition but lets you attach a custom class and arbitrary data,
which turns an error from something a human reads into something
code downstream can also catch and act on. `check_stratum()` below
validates `ef_stratum` against the HF-HOME codebook and, on
failure, reports which values were unrecognized as structured data,
not only as text embedded in a message:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(rlang)

check_stratum <- function(x) {
  valid <- c("Reduced EF", "Preserved EF")
  bad <- setdiff(unique(x), valid)
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    abort(
      message = paste0("unrecognized ef_stratum value(s): ",
                       paste(bad, collapse = ", ")),
      class = "hf_bad_stratum",
      bad_values = bad
    )
  }
  invisible(x)
}

check_stratum(hf_rand$ef_stratum)   # the real column: passes silently
```
:::


A corrupted copy, with one stratum written in lower case, triggers
the error; catching it by class rather than by parsing the message
recovers the exact offending values as data:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
corrupted <- c(hf_rand$ef_stratum, "reduced ef")
caught <- tryCatch(
  check_stratum(corrupted),
  hf_bad_stratum = function(e) e
)
class(caught)
#> [1] "hf_bad_stratum" "rlang_error"    "error"          "condition"
caught$bad_values
#> [1] "reduced ef"
```
:::


The base equivalent is possible but more work: `stop()` takes only
text, so catching a specific kind of error by anything other than
matching a substring of the message requires wrapping the condition
yourself with `structure(class = c("hf_bad_stratum", "error",
"condition"), ...)`, which `abort()` does for you, correctly,
every time. A caller that wants to catch only `hf_bad_stratum`
errors and let every other error propagate writes `tryCatch(expr,
hf_bad_stratum = handler)`; matching on a message substring instead
breaks the moment the wording changes, which is exactly the kind of
brittle test @sec-testing-smells warns against, now in production
code rather than a test file.

**What `rlang::last_trace()` adds.** `traceback()` shows the raw
call stack; `rlang::last_trace()`, called after an `abort()`-raised
error, shows the same information with the tree structure of nested
calls made visible and `abort()`'s own data payload accessible on
the condition object it stores:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
check_stratum(corrupted)
#> Error in `check_stratum()`:
#> ! unrecognized ef_stratum value(s): reduced ef
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
last_trace()
#> <error/hf_bad_stratum>
#> Error in `check_stratum()`:
#> ! unrecognized ef_stratum value(s): reduced ef
#> ---
#> Backtrace:
#>     x
#>  1. \-global check_stratum(corrupted)
#> Run rlang::last_trace(drop = FALSE) to see 1 hidden frame.
```
:::


The indentation in `last_trace()`'s output tracks which call was
made from inside which other call, which matters once a validation
helper like `check_stratum()` is itself called from inside a
cleaning pipeline several layers deep; `traceback()`'s flat,
most-recent-first list carries the same information but requires
you to reconstruct the nesting yourself from indentation that is not
there.

This is Habit 8 in code, not only in prose: a stratum value quietly
miscoded would not stop the pipeline if nothing asserts what the
valid values are, and the pipeline would continue to a plausible,
wrong summary. `check_stratum()` is the assertion that turns that
quiet failure into a loud one, with enough structure in the error
(`bad_values`, a specific `class`) that a caller can decide
automatically whether to stop, warn, or drop the offending rows,
rather than only print a message for a human to read.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**A caught error you do not re-raise or log has simply vanished.**
`tryCatch(risky_step(), error = function(e) NULL)` makes a failure
disappear as completely as the `NULL`-returning function at the
start of this chapter did, only on purpose this time. Catch an
error only when you have a specific recovery in mind for it (a
default value, a retry, a skip with a recorded reason); otherwise
let it propagate.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** `abort()`'s `class` argument accepts a character
vector, not just one string, for example `class = c("hf_bad_stratum", "hf_validation_error")`.
What does giving it two classes let a caller do that one class does
not?

**Answer.** A `tryCatch()` handler matches on any class a condition
has, so a caller interested only in HF-HOME validation errors in
general can catch `hf_validation_error` and handle every specific
kind of validation failure (bad stratum, bad sex code, bad date)
the same way, while a caller that cares specifically about the
stratum problem can still catch `hf_bad_stratum` alone. One string
forces every caller to know the exact, specific class; a small
hierarchy lets callers choose how broadly to catch.
:::

### Exercises

7. Rewrite `check_stratum()`'s base-R equivalent using `stop()` and
   `structure()` so that a caller can still catch it by class as
   `"hf_bad_stratum"`, without using `rlang`. Compare the line count
   with the `abort()` version.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
check_stratum_base <- function(x) {
  valid <- c("Reduced EF", "Preserved EF")
  bad <- setdiff(unique(x), valid)
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    cond <- structure(
      class = c("hf_bad_stratum", "error", "condition"),
      list(message = paste0("unrecognized ef_stratum value(s): ",
                            paste(bad, collapse = ", ")),
           call = sys.call(-1), bad_values = bad)
    )
    stop(cond)
  }
  invisible(x)
}
caught_base <- tryCatch(check_stratum_base(corrupted),
                        hf_bad_stratum = function(e) e)
caught_base$bad_values
#> [1] "reduced ef"
```
:::


The base version does the same job in roughly the same number of
lines, but every piece, the three-element class vector, the
`message` and `call` fields a condition object must have, is a
detail `abort()` supplies by default. The cost is not length; it is
that each of those details is a place to get the base version
subtly wrong (forgetting `"condition"` from the class vector breaks
`tryCatch()` entirely, silently, until someone tries to catch it).
:::

## Testing functions in isolation {#sec-functions-testing}

Every function in this chapter has been called directly, on a
data frame built for the purpose, rather than only inside the
pipeline that would normally call it: `site_event_rate_strict()`
has been exercised with the full `hf_events` table, with a vector
of mismatched labels, and, below, with a four-row fixture built by
hand. That is the point @sec-testing-unit makes at length and this
section only connects to, rather than repeats: a function is far
easier to get right, and far easier to debug when it is wrong, when
its tests call it directly, with inputs you chose, than when the
only evidence of its behavior is whatever the full pipeline happens
to produce from this week's data.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tinytest)

fixture <- data.frame(
  site = c("Site A", "Site A", "Site B"),
  event_30d = c(1, 0, NA)
)
out <- site_event_rate_strict(fixture, "Site A")
expect_equal(out$n, 2, info = "both Site A rows counted")
#> ----- PASSED      : <-->
#>  call| expect_equal(out$n, 2, info = "both Site A rows counted")
#>  info| both Site A rows counted
expect_equal(out$event_rate, 0.5, info = "one of two ascertained events")
#> ----- PASSED      : <-->
#>  call| expect_equal(out$event_rate, 0.5, info = "one of two ascertained events")
#>  info| one of two ascertained events
expect_error(site_event_rate_strict(fixture, "Site Z"),
             pattern = "no rows found",
             info = "a site absent from the fixture errors, not NULL")
#> ----- PASSED      : <-->
#>  call| expect_error(site_event_rate_strict(fixture, "Site Z"), pattern = "no rows found", 
#>  call| info = "a site absent from the fixture errors, not NULL")
#>  info| a site absent from the fixture errors, not NULL
```
:::


The third assertion is the one this chapter's opening bug did not
have: a test that an unmatched site raises an error, run against
the *strict* version, would have failed the moment someone wrote it
against the original `site_event_rate()`, which returns `NULL`
instead, long before that function ever reached a loop over five
site labels copied from the wrong table. Writing that test does not
require the pipeline, the join, or any file on disk; it requires
only the function and a few rows built to exercise exactly the
branch in question, which is the broader argument of this section:
isolate the function from everything around it before you decide
whether it is correct, then let the integration layer of
@sec-testing-correctness confirm that the isolated pieces still
compose correctly once wired together.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** The fixture above has `event_30d = NA` for one row
and the test checks `event_rate == 0.5`. Does this test the
function's handling of missing outcomes, or only its handling of
complete ones?

**Answer.** It tests the handling of missing outcomes directly:
`mean(c(1, 0, NA), na.rm = TRUE)` is `0.5`, computed from the two
non-missing rows, so the assertion passes only if `na.rm = TRUE`
is actually in effect inside the function. Deleting `na.rm = TRUE`
from `site_event_rate_strict()` would make this same fixture return
`NA` for `event_rate`, and the test would fail, which is exactly
what distinguishes a test with a deliberately missing value in its
fixture from one built only from complete rows.
:::

#> ----- PASSED      : <-->

`expect_silent()` is the right assertion for 'raises no error', not
`expect_true(TRUE)` after a bare call: `expect_silent()` fails if
the call produces an error, a warning, or even a message, which is
closer to the actual claim ('the real column is clean') than merely
confirming the function returned at all.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **A function is one place to fix a bug.** Write a function the
   first time a computation would otherwise be copied, not the
   third; the cost of writing it is small and the cost of finding
   four copies of a bug later is not.
2. **A closure freezes a snapshot, not a live reference.** If a
   function factory's returned function seems to be using stale
   data, suspect that the data it closed over changed after the
   closure was created, not that the closure is reading something
   live.
3. **`map()` over `for` or `sapply()` when the length or type of the
   result matters.** `map()` always returns a list the same length
   as its input; a `for` loop assigning a possibly-`NULL` value with
   `[[<-` can silently shrink, and `sapply()`'s return type depends
   on what the calls happen to return.
4. **Habit 8: make the quiet failure loud.** A function that returns
   `NULL`, or a mean computed over the wrong rows, produces a
   plausible-looking answer with no error; `rlang::abort()` with a
   class and a data payload turns a violated assumption into a
   condition code can catch, not only a message a human might miss.
5. **Test a function directly before trusting what the pipeline
   says about it.** A fixture built by hand, with the one edge case
   you are worried about, finds a bug in minutes that the full
   pipeline, run on this week's data, might never happen to exercise
   at all.

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Code | Guards against |
|---|---|---|
| Define a function with a default | `f <- function(x, y = 1) x + y` | Repeating an argument's usual value at every call site |
| Forward extra arguments | `f <- function(x, ...) g(x, ...)` | Re-naming every option a wrapped function accepts |
| Return early | `if (bad) return(NA)` | An implicit `NULL` from a conditional with no `else` |
| Make a closure | `function(data) function(x) ...` | A function needing a global variable it should not depend on |
| Inspect a closure's captured value | `environment(f)$data` | Assuming a closure reads a name 'live' |
| Iterate, preserving length and type | `purrr::map(x, f)` | A `for` loop or `sapply()` silently shrinking or changing type |
| Iterate numeric results | `purrr::map_dbl(x, f)` | A list where a numeric vector was expected |
| Catch errors per element | `purrr::possibly(f, otherwise = NA)` | A `for` loop stopping at the first failure |
| Catch errors, keep the reason | `purrr::safely(f)` | Losing which inputs failed and why |
| See the call stack after an error | `traceback()` | Guessing which function actually failed |
| Pause inside a function, every call | `browser()` inside the body | Not knowing what to add until you see the state |
| Pause once, no file edit | `debugonce(f)` | A `browser()` call left behind in committed code |
| Pause at the first uncaught error, any function | `options(error = recover)` | Having to guess which function to instrument first |
| Raise a catchable, data-carrying error | `rlang::abort(msg, class = "...", data = ...)` | A `stop()` message a caller can only parse as text |
| See a readable, nested call tree | `rlang::last_trace()` | Reconstructing nesting from a flat `traceback()` |
| Test one function, not the pipeline | A hand-built fixture plus `tinytest::expect_*()` | A bug the full pipeline happens not to exercise |

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-14b}

1. The value of the last expression evaluated in the function's
   body, whether or not that expression is the last line written: a
   conditional with no matching branch, for instance, evaluates to
   `NULL`, and that `NULL` is what the function returns even though
   no line in it says `return(NULL)`.
2. `purrr::map()` stores each call's result as an element of a
   preallocated-length list, so a `NULL` result occupies its own
   position, visible, rather than being omitted. A `for` loop that
   assigns with `result[[i]] <- f(x[i])` uses `[[<-` assignment,
   under which assigning `NULL` *deletes* that list element instead
   of storing it, so the loop can finish having silently produced a
   shorter list than the number of iterations it ran.
3. `rlang::abort()` lets an error carry a custom class (so a caller
   can catch exactly that kind of failure with `tryCatch()`, rather
   than parsing the message text) and arbitrary named data (so the
   caller can recover structured information about what went wrong,
   such as which specific values were invalid, rather than only a
   human-readable sentence). It is for turning a violated
   assumption into something code downstream can act on
   automatically, not only something a person reading the console
   can react to.
